IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF BOND MEASURE Z

This Impartial Analysis of Bond Measure Z has been prepared by County Counsel pursuant to Section 9500
of the California Elections Code.
This Measure was placed on the ballot by a resolution adopted by the Board of Education of the San Bernardino City
Unified School District (District). A "yes" vote by at least fifty-five percent of the voters voting on this Measure will
authorize the District to issue bonds in the amount of up to $345,000,000 to be used solely for the purposes set forth in
this ballot Measure. A "no" vote means that the District will not be authorized to issue and sell the up to $345,000,000 in
bonds set forth in the Measure.
The District's Resolution was adopted pursuant to California Education Code sections 5304, 5322, 15100 et seq., 15266,
and Articles XIIIA and XVI of the California Constitution. The bond proceeds may only be used for specific projects listed
in the "Bond Project List." The "Bond Project List" section contains the specific projects the District proposes to finance
with proceeds from the sale of the bonds authorized by this ballot Measure and the bond proceeds may only be used for
those specific projects. These projects include: renovation and construction projects to replace portable classrooms with
permanent facilities; construction or acquiring and installing additional classrooms; modernizing all classrooms for current
educational standards, including upgrading technology equipment; improvement to school grounds to create innovative
indoor and outdoor learning areas; construction, replacement, improvement, renovation, or acquisition and installation of
restrooms, warming kitchens, Early Learning Centers, Transitional Kindergarten facilities, Career Technical Education
classrooms, auditoriums, performing arts classrooms, physical education facilities, green spaces, playgrounds, playfields,
and other projects; energy-efficient upgrades to equipment; construction of a new school to reduce overcrowding; and
various other projects. Some of the projects listed in the Measure may assume the receipt of matching State funds which
may or may not be approved by the State Legislature.
The District will conduct financial and performance audits annually and all bond expenditures will be monitored by an
Independent Citizens' Oversight Committee to ensure that the bond proceeds are spent as promised and specified as
required by Education Code section 15278 et seq. in order to ensure bond revenues are used for proper purposes and
that no funds are used for any teacher or administrative salaries or other operating expenses. No District employees or
vendors will be allowed to serve on the Citizens' Oversight Committee. The District will also take all actions necessary to
establish an account in which proceeds from the bond measure will be deposited in accordance with state law.
The bonded debt will be a general obligation of the District and will be financed by taxes levied annually on taxable
property located within the District.
LAURA FEINGOLD
County Counsel
s/ JOLENA E. GRIDER
Deputy County Counsel

County Counsel’s Impartial Analysis

                                            Measure B

                               Beaumont Unified School District


The purpose of Measure B is to enable voters to authorize or reject the Beaumont Unified School
District (“District”) issuing and selling bonds to provide financing for school facilities projects.
The Board of Trustees of the District, by adopting Resolution No. 2026-27-03 (“Resolution”),
elected to call an election to place this Measure on the ballot.

Measure B would enable the District to issue and sell bonds of up to a maximum of eighty six
million ($86,000,000), at legal rates, levying 2¢ per $100 (or $20 per $100,000) of assessed value
while the bonds are outstanding. This Measure, if approved, will not increase current tax rates.
Money raised by the sale of the bonds must be used exclusively to finance the list of projects
described in the full text of Measure B, which is included in this voter information pamphlet. Bond
proceeds will be expended on improvements of deteriorating roofs; plumbing; HVAC; electrical;
safety systems; repair/upgrade aging classrooms; science labs; school/career technology facilities
at existing schools to support college/career readiness in health sciences, engineering, and skilled
trades. Monies generated by the sale of such bonds shall only be spent for these specified purposes.
Bond proceeds cannot be expended to finance teacher and administrator salaries or other school
operating expenses.

Measure B provides for the District to establish an independent citizens’ oversight committee to
ensure bonds proceeds are expended only on the types of school facilities projects that have been
listed on the ballot pamphlet. The District will conduct an annual, independent performance and
financial audits to oversee that bond proceeds have been expended only on the school facilities
projects listed.

For this Measure to be approved, at least 55% of qualified voters within the District who vote on
the Measure must vote yes.

A “YES” vote on Measure “B” is a vote to authorize the District to issue and sell bonds to provide
financing of school facilities projects.

A “NO” VOTE on Measure “B” is a vote to reject the District from issuing and selling bonds to
prove financing of school facilities projects.

measures.officialStatement:
CITYATTORNEY'S IMPARTIALANALYSIS OF MEASURE _____

The City Council of the City of Needles has placed Measure __ on the ballot for the November
3, 2026 General Municipal Election. Measure __ would amend Section 503 of the City Charter
to increase the compensation paid to each member of the City Council from one dollar ($1.00)
per month to one hundred fifty dollars ($150.00) per month.

Effect of Measure on Existing Law:

The City of Needles is a charter city operating under a City Charter adopted by the voters in
1958. Section 503 of the Charter currently provides that each member of the City Council shall
receive compensation in the amount of one dollar ($1.00) per month. That amount has remained
unchanged since the Charter was adopted approximately sixty-eight years ago.

Because the amount of City Council compensation is established by the City Charter, it may not
be changed by ordinance or resolution of the City Council. Under the California Constitution and
applicable law governing charter cities, any amendment to the Charter, including a change to
City Council compensation, must be approved by the voters.

If approved, Measure __ would amend Section 503 of the City Charter to establish compensation
for each City Council Member at one hundred fifty dollars ($150.00) per month. The measure
would not modify any other provision of Section 503. Existing Charter provisions authorizing
reimbursement for actual and necessary travel and other official expenses incurred in the
performance of official duties would remain unchanged. The measure would not authorize any
additional salary, benefits, or compensation beyond that expressly provided in the Charter.

 If approved, the City has determined Measure ___ would result in an additional annual cost of
$20,916 to the City. Pursuant to State law, approval of Measure ___ requires a majority vote of
the City’s voters who vote in the election.

If approved, the amendment would become effective following certification of the election
results and completion of all procedures required by law for charter amendments.

A "Yes" vote is a vote in favor of amending Section 503 of the City Charter to increase City
Council compensation from one dollar ($1.00) per month to one hundred fifty dollars ($150.00)
per month.

A "No" vote is a vote against the proposed Charter amendment, and Section 503 of the City
Charter would remain unchanged, with City Council compensation continuing at one dollar
($1.00) per month.

The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure _____. If you desire a copy of the Measure,
please call the City Clerk's office at (760 ) 326-2113 and a copy will be mailed at no cost to you, or
you may obtain a copy by visiting the City's website at www.cityofneedles.com

                                                       Lena D. Wade
                                                       Deputy City Attorney

measures.officialStatement:
CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS
This Impartial Analysis of Measure __ has been prepared by the City Attorney pursuant to Section
9280 of the California Elections Code.

On June 9, 2026, the Highland City Council unanimously voted to place Measure __ on the
November ballot. If approved by the voters, Measure __ would authorize a one percent (1%) retail
transactions and use tax (“Sales Tax Ordinance”) within the City of Highland. This would increase
the City’s existing sales tax rate by 1%, or 1 cent, on every dollar of taxable sales of goods in the
City, and on the taxable storage, use or consumption of goods purchased in the City. The Sales
Tax Ordinance would remain effective until ended by the voters.

This sales tax would be a “general tax,” meaning that revenues raised from the tax would go into
the City’s general fund to pay for any lawful City program, improvement, or service. City staff
have estimated that the Sales Tax Ordinance will raise approximately $6.35 million in local
revenue. The City Council’s adopted ballot question states the revenue from Measure _ would be
used to fund police, fire, and emergency services, and repair critical infrastructure such as roads,
bridges, and interchanges, including the 5th Street Corridor Interchange, among other public
improvements.

Similar to other sales tax revenue, the State of California will collect revenue generated by the
Measure under a contract with the City, and will pay the revenue over to the City. The City’s
budget process and annual independent audit, as well as the City’s Annual Comprehensive
Financial Report and other publicly available documents, will provide accountability over revenue
and expenditures from the Sales Tax Ordinance. The total sales tax rate paid in the City of
Highland, which includes the sales tax collected for the State of California, San Bernardino
County, and other public agencies, is currently 7.75%. If voters approve the Measure, the total
sales tax rate paid in the City would be 8.75%. Sales tax is not collected on certain exempt items
such as prescription medications or groceries.

Article XIIIC of the California Constitution, commonly known as Proposition 218, requires that
a majority of the voters voting on a general tax measure adopt the Sales Tax Ordinance for it to
take effect. A “yes” vote on Measure __ is to adopt the Sales Tax Ordinance. A “no” vote on
Measure __ is to not adopt the Sales Tax Ordinance.


Maricela Marroquin
Highland City Attorney

The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure __. If you desire a complete copy
of the Sales Tax Ordinance, please call the City Clerk at (909) 864-6861 and a copy will be
sent to you at no cost.

CHINO BUSINESS LICENSE TAX MEASURE
                       CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS

Measure __ was placed on the ballot by the Chino City Council. If approved by a majority of voters
voting on the measure, it would adopt an ordinance adding Chapter 3.44 to the Chino Municipal
Code and repealing related existing business license tax provisions.

The City currently imposes a business license tax on businesses operating in the City. The measure
would replace portions of the existing business license tax structure with a gross receipts-based
tax. The tax would apply to gross receipts attributable to business activity conducted in the City.

For businesses with $75,000 or less in gross receipts, the tax would be $25. For gross receipts
above $75,000, the measure would impose the following maximum tax rates on gross receipts
above $75,000:

General/retail businesses: $0.60 per $1,000
Contractors: $1.00 per $1,000
Services: $1.00 per $1,000
Professional/advanced businesses: $1.50 per $1,000
Real property/rental businesses: $1.50 per $1,000
The measure would authorize the City to administer, collect, and enforce the business license tax,
including through rules, procedures, audits, determinations, penalties, interest, refund procedures,
and collection remedies, as provided in the ordinance. The City Council could adopt implementing
rules and make amendments to administer the ordinance, clarify procedures, correct errors,
conform the ordinance to law, or reduce, suspend, or repeal the tax. The City Council could not,
without further voter approval, increase any tax rate above the voter-approved maximum rate,
expand the tax to persons or activities not subject to the tax, or otherwise increase the tax in a
manner requiring voter approval.

The measure is a general tax. Revenue from the tax would be deposited into the City’s General
Fund and could be used for any lawful municipal purpose. The measure states that revenue may
be used for general City services, including police and 911 emergency response, streets, public
area safety and cleanliness, protecting local drinking water sources, and other general City
services. The measure does not legally restrict the use of revenues to those purposes.

If the measure is approved, the ordinance would be considered adopted when the City Council
declares the election results and would become operative on the date specified in the ordinance. If
the measure is not approved by a majority of voters voting on it, the ordinance would not be
adopted and would have no force or effect.

A “Yes” vote is a vote to approve the business license tax ordinance.

A “No” vote is a vote against approving the business license tax ordinance.

CITY OF TWENTYNINE PALMS
                 CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE “___”
                    ONE PERCENT TRANSACTIONS AND USE (SALES) TAX

On July 14, 2026, the City Council voted to place Measure “___” on the November 3, 2026 general
municipal election ballot to seek voter approval of an ordinance enacting a one percent transactions
and use tax locally in the City of Twentynine Palms (City), referred to herein by its common name a
“Sales Tax.” Such taxes are not taxes on homes or properties, and rather are applied to purchases
(with exceptions for items such as groceries or prescription medication). As a result, the proposed
Sales Tax will apply equally to anyone making an applicable purchase, including tourists and other
visitors.

If approved by a majority of Twentynine Palms voters, this Measure would implement a one percent
“sales tax” on applicable transactions within the City. The “sales tax” will be calculated based on the
sales price of tangible personal property sold at retail in the City. For example, for every $100 spent on
taxable goods, the proposed tax would be one dollar ($1.00).

The stated “Purpose” of the Measure is “to create a locally-controlled funding source, which is legally
protected from being taken by the State, by creating a 1% transaction (sales) and use tax, the proceeds

                        CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS

                        TRANSIENT OCCUPANCY TAX MEASURE

Existing Law:

The City Council of the City of Needles has placed Measure __ on the ballot for the November
3, 2026 General Municipal Election. Measure __ would amend sections 20-8, 20-9, and 20-10 of
the Needles City Code to increase the City's transient occupancy tax ("TOT") from its current
rate of ten percent (10%) to fourteen percent (14%) through a phased implementation.

Effect of Measure on Existing Law:

The City's transient occupancy tax is imposed on the rent charged for occupancy of hotels,
motels, recreational vehicle parks, short-term residential rental units, and other lodging
establishments within the City for stays of 30 days or less. Although hotel and lodging operators
collect and remit the tax to the City, the tax is paid by the transient occupant rather than the
property owner or operator.

Currently, the City's transient occupancy tax rate is ten percent (10%). If approved by the voters,
Measure __ would increase the tax rate in the following phases:

   -- Effective January 1, 2027, the tax rate would increase to twelve percent (12%);
   -- Effective January 1, 2029, the tax rate would increase to thirteen percent (13%); and
   -- Effective January 1, 2030, the tax rate would increase to fourteen percent (14%).

The measure would also amend related provisions of the Needles City Code governing the
monthly reporting and remittance of the tax by lodging operators and the calculation of penalties
for delinquent reports and payments to reflect the applicable tax rate in effect at the time the tax
is due.

Measure __ would impose a general tax. Revenues generated by the measure would be deposited
into the City's General Fund and may be used for any lawful municipal purpose as determined by
the City Council through the annual budget process. The measure itself does not dedicate the
additional revenues to any particular program, project, or service.

If approved, the increased tax rates would apply beginning on the effective dates specified above
and would remain in effect unless subsequently amended or repealed in accordance with
applicable law.

Based on current lodging activity, if approved, the City has determined that Measure ___ would
generate approximately $200,000 annually beginning in 2027, $300,000 annually beginning in
2029, and approximately $400,000 annually upon full implementation beginning in 2030.
 Because Measure __ would enact a general tax, it requires approval by a majority of the voters
voting on the measure to become effective.

A "Yes" vote is a vote in favor of increasing the City's transient occupancy tax from ten percent
(10%) to fourteen percent (14%) through phased increases beginning January 1, 2027.
A "No" vote is a vote against the measure, and the transient occupancy tax would remain at ten
percent (10%).

CITY OF UPLAND
       CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE “M”
         THE “UPLAND BUSINESS LICENSE REFORM MEASURE”
ADJUSTING THE RATES OF BUSINESS LICENSE TAXES WITHIN THE CITY AND
                MAKING OTHER TECHNICAL UPDATES

For decades, the City of Upland has levied a license tax on businesses operating within the City.
The business license tax is a general tax. Revenues are deposited into the General Fund and may
be spent for any City expense, like street repair, infrastructure repair and maintenance,
emergency response, and public safety. The existing license tax structure was last updated in
1994. Because the existing structure treats most businesses with gross receipts over $1,400,001
identically, capping the amount of the tax at $864, the structure taxes small businesses at a higher
proportional rate while taxing larger businesses at a lower proportional rate.

On August 3, 2026, the City Council unanimously voted to place Measure “M” on the November
3, 2026 ballot. If approved by majority (50%+1) of Upland voters, this Measure would revise
the City’s business license tax to be based predominantly on gross receipts rather than a range of
factors, including number of employees. For small businesses with less than $100,000 in annual
gross receipts, the business license tax shall be a flat $75.00 per year. For annual gross receipts
over $100,000, the rates for each business classification would be:

   •   Retail/Commercial: 0.065%;

   •   Contractors: 0.150%;

   •   Rental (commercial or residential): 0.200%;

   •   General Service (nonprofessional or non-semiprofessional, e.g., hair and nail salons):
       0.125%; and

   •   Professional service/calling or semiprofessional: 0.125%.

In addition, self-storage facilities would pay $50 per unit.

Notwithstanding the above, the maximum business license tax would be capped at $28,000 per
business per year. With the larger cap, the proposed measure would result in larger businesses
paying a greater proportional share relative to small businesses than they do under the current
structure.

The Measure would continue to exempt businesses exempted by Federal or State law along with
any person issued a special event permit who does not have a fixed place of business and is not
otherwise engaged in business within the City.

The Measure also updates the City’s tax collection and administrative procedures. This includes
updating definitions, license application, review, denial, approval, renewal and transfer
procedures, tax calculation formulas, and tax deficiency, credit, refund and appeal procedures.
Proceeds from the tax will be subject to an annual, independent financial audit, and audit results
 shall be available to the public.

This tax is estimated to generate $3.3 million annually, $2.1 million more than the current
business license tax structure. The new rates would become effective on January 1, 2028 and
remain in effect until repealed by voters. From January 1, 2027 until December 31, 2027, the
business license tax will be levied at a rate temporarily lowered by 0.005%-0.075%.

A “yes” vote on Measure “M” will approve this amendment to the City’s business license tax
code.

A “no” vote on Measure “M” will not approve this amendment to the City’s business license tax
code.

The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure “M”. If you desire a copy of the
Measure, please call the City’s elections official at (909) 931-4120 and a copy will be mailed
at no cost to you.

On July 28, 2026, the Grand Terrace City Council voted to place Measure N, entitled the “Grand

election ballot.

If approved by a majority of voters, the Measure would add Chapter 3.32 to the City of Grand
Terrace Municipal Code, establishing a one percent (1.00%) transactions and use tax (commonly
known as a “sales tax”) for City general fund purposes.

State law allows certain entities, including municipalities, to increase sales tax within their
jurisdictions if approved by the voters. If approved, the Measure would impose a 1.00% tax upon
retailers’ gross receipts from the retail sale of most tangible personal property sold within the City,
and to the storage, use, or other consumption within the City of most tangible personal property
purchased from retailers.

It is estimated that this tax will generate approximately $1,200,000 annually in revenue. Funds

                   •   Law enforcement services,

                   •   Responding to non-emergency calls for service,

                   •   Funding general public services provided by the City.

Food purchased as groceries and prescription medication, among other common essentials, would
not be taxed under the Measure. Visitors to Grand Terrace would bear part of the tax burden
imposed by their local activities and thus contribute to the City’s ability to maintain general public
services they use while visiting. Residents and other purchasers of goods in the City would also be
subject to the tax. The specific retail sales and uses subject to the tax would be determined under
California Department of Tax and Fee Administration (“CDTFA”) regulations and the CDTFA
would administer the tax under contract with the City of Grand Terrace.

The Measure includes accountability provisions, including the creation of an Advisory Committee
to review revenues and expenditures of the tax and review annual audit reports related to the tax,
and make at least one written annual report to the City Council summarizing findings and including
any appropriate recommendations.

While the ordinance permits future amendments by the City Council, any tax increase must be
approved by voters. The transactions and use tax proposed by the Measure would take effect only

Measure "__" passes, the City Treasurer would be appointed by the Colton City Council
and no longer elected by Colton voters. If Colton voters approve Measure "__", the City

expires in November, 2028.

last elected in November, 2024, is currently occupied by Mr. Michael Razo, and will
expire in November, 2028. California law requires that general law cities, like Colton,
have either an elected or appointed City Treasurer. However, a transition from an elected
City Treasurer to an appointed City Treasurer must be approved by a majority of the
City’s voters voting at an election. If Measure "__" passes and the position becomes
appointed, the City Council will decide the minimum education and training requirements
for the position and periodically review the City Treasurer’s performance.

appointed position and no election for the City Treasurer’s Office would be held in
November, 2028 or future years unless and until changed again by Colton voters via

CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE __


This ballot measure establishes a local transactions and use tax in the City of Adelanto. The
ballot measure amends the Adelanto Municipal Code to add Chapter 3.70 to include the tax.
It is estimated that the tax will raise approximately $3,000,000 for the City of Adelanto. All
funds raised would go to the City’s General Fund and could be used for any legitimate municipal
purpose including, but not limited to, repairing and improving streets and infrastructure such as
storm drains, sidewalks and public facilities, maintaining parks and public areas, fire protection,
paramedic and emergency response services, public safety and crime prevention efforts,
homelessness response activities, and other municipal services identified through the annual
City budget process.
A transactions tax is generally known as a sales tax. The sales tax is imposed on all retailers
within the City of Adelanto at the rate of 1% (one percent) of the gross receipts of the retailer
from the sale of all tangible personal property sold within the City.
The use tax is similar to a sales tax and it applies when one purchases an item from a retailer
outside of the City of Adelanto that does not collect sales tax. The use tax is at the rate of 1%
(one percent) of the sales price of the property and includes delivery charges when such
charges are subject to state sales or use taxes. Use taxes are charged in order to treat
transactions equally and not penalize local retailers that are subject to a sales tax.
Any transaction is only charged a sales or use tax and not both taxes. The 1% (one percent) tax
is only charged once to any transaction. The tax is not only on transactions involving City
residents, but the tax is also charged on transactions by non-residents that occur within the
City.
The tax is not charged to transactions that are exempt from such taxation under applicable law.
If approved, the tax would go into effect April 1, 2027.
The proceeds of the tax shall be subject to an annual audit by an independent certified public
accountant and the results of the audit shall be reported to the City Council in a document
posted on the City’s website and available for public inspection.
The measure will be adopted if a majority of voters who vote on the measure vote to approve
the measure.
The measure was placed on the ballot by the Adelanto City Council.
 The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure __. If you desire a copy of the
measure, please call the City Clerk’s office at 760-246-2300 x11123 and a copy will be mailed at
no cost to you.


Todd Litfin, City Attorney

provenance.quote: Shall the measure to provide funding for Adelanto city services, such as paving streets and fixing potholes, fire protection, paramedic, and 911 response; law enforcement and crime prevention; keeping public areas/parks safe/clean; addressing homelessness; and repairing aging storm drains, pipes, bridges, and public areas by establishing a 1% transactions and use tax, providing approximately $3,000,000 annually until ended by voters, requiring audits, public spending disclosure, all money controlled locally, be adopted?

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Authorize up to $345 million in bonds for classrooms, laboratories, career-technology and school facilities, roofs, plumbing, heating and cooling, electrical systems, safety and disabled access, including the listed new-school and classroom projects. Property taxes on taxable property in the district would repay principal and interest. The district estimates $22 million annually, an average rate of $45 and highest rate of $45 per $100,000 of assessed value, collection through fiscal year 2056–57, and approximately $670,286,938 total repayment. These are estimates that may vary, not guaranteed tax caps or repayment amounts. Interest rates must stay within legal limits. Money must remain local and be spent on the listed facility projects. Bond proceeds cannot pay teacher or administrator salaries or other operating expenses. Independent citizen oversight and annual financial and performance audits are required. Some projects may depend on state matching funds that are not guaranteed. Approval requires 55% of votes.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Authorize the district to borrow up to $345 million for the listed facilities and levy property taxes to repay the bonds under these conditions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not authorize these bonds through this measure.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Authorize up to $236.7 million in bonds for classroom, restroom, career-technical and other school facilities, roof repairs, safety and security, and electrical, plumbing and sewer systems. Property taxes on taxable property in the district would repay principal and interest. The district estimates $14.2 million annually, an average rate of $47.46 and highest rate of $49 per $100,000 of assessed value, collection through fiscal year 2062–63, and approximately $511.36 million total repayment. These are estimates that may vary, not guaranteed tax caps or repayment amounts. Interest rates must stay within legal limits. Money must remain local and be spent on the listed facility projects. Money cannot pay teacher or administrator salaries unrelated to project oversight, or other operating expenses. Independent citizen oversight and annual financial and performance audits are required. The ballot question describes an approximate $47.50 rate. Some projects may depend on other funding; not every listed project is guaranteed. Approval requires 55% of votes.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Authorize the district to borrow up to $236.7 million for the listed facilities and levy property taxes to repay the bonds under these conditions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not authorize these bonds through this measure.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Authorize up to $86 million in bonds for school roofs, plumbing, heating and cooling, electrical systems, safety, classrooms, laboratories and career-technology facilities. Property taxes on taxable property in the district would repay principal and interest. The district estimates $6 million annually, an average rate of $20 and highest rate of $20 per $100,000 of assessed value, collection through fiscal year 2056–57, and approximately $178 million total repayment. These are estimates that may vary, not guaranteed tax caps or repayment amounts. Interest rates must stay within legal limits. Money must remain local and be spent on the listed facility projects. Bond proceeds cannot pay teacher or administrator salaries or other operating expenses. Independent citizen oversight and annual financial and performance audits are required. The district plans to maintain the current tax rate through its bond schedule; actual rates and timing may change. Some projects may need state matching funds that are not guaranteed. Approval requires 55% of votes.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Authorize the district to borrow up to $86 million for the listed facilities and levy property taxes to repay the bonds under these conditions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not authorize these bonds through this measure.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Increase each Needles City Council member’s compensation from $1 to $150 per month by amending the city charter. Reimbursement for actual and necessary official travel and expenses would remain available, and the amendment would not create other compensation or benefits beyond those allowed by the charter. The city attorney estimates $20,916 in additional annual city spending. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the increase to $150 per member per month.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Add a 1% Highland sales and use tax, or $1 per $100 of taxable purchases, increasing the current combined rate from 7.75% to 8.75%. Groceries and prescription medicines remain exempt. The city estimates $6.35 million annually for its general fund, available for any lawful city service, including police, fire, roads and other infrastructure; those examples are not binding earmarks. Annual independent audits are required. Collection would begin in the first calendar quarter more than 110 days after adoption, subject to the state administration agreement. The tax would continue until voters repeal it. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional 1% local sales and use tax under these rules.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not add this proposed 1% tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Replace parts of Chino’s business-license tax with a tax on gross receipts from business conducted in the city, starting January 1, 2027 unless law requires another date. Businesses with $75,000 or less in receipts would pay $25. Above that amount, the tax would be $25 plus a category rate on receipts exceeding $75,000: $0.60 per $1,000 for general or retail businesses; $1 for contractors and services; and $1.50 for professional or advanced businesses and real-property or rental businesses. Revenue would go to the general fund for any lawful city purpose, with annual independent audits and public reporting. This taxes business activity, not residency alone. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the new business-license tax structure and its administration rules.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this replacement business-license tax ordinance; existing business-license tax provisions would remain.

parts.label: Exemptions and mixed businesses
parts.what: Federal and state tax exemptions and qualifying nonprofit, religious and government exemptions remain. State-required fees are separate. Receipts from different business categories may be reasonably allocated; if they cannot be, the highest applicable rate applies.

parts.label: Future changes
parts.what: The council could reduce, suspend, repeal or restore the tax within the approved maximum and make administrative amendments. Increasing the approved rates or expanding taxable persons or activities would require voter approval.

parts.label: Conflicting official revenue estimates
parts.what: The ordered ballot question estimates $4.8 million annually. The ordinance’s recital estimates $5.9 million. Actual collections may vary; the two official documents do not give the same estimate.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Add a 1% Twentynine Palms sales and use tax, or $1 per $100 of taxable purchases, expected to begin April 1, 2027. Groceries and prescription medicines would remain exempt. The city estimates $2 million annually for local services and priorities such as emergency response, police, streets, flood and disaster response, parks and the animal shelter. Although this is a general tax, the ordinance requires spending to further its stated local-service purpose. The annual audit must check that restriction, summarize spending and make the summary public. The tax has no fixed expiration and would continue until lawfully ended. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional 1% tax and its local-purpose and audit requirements.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not add this proposed 1% tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Add a 0.5% Ontario sales and use tax, or 50 cents per $100 of taxable purchases, in addition to current sales taxes. Collection would start April 1, 2027. The city estimates $32.5 million annually for its general fund, available for any lawful city program or service, including emergency response, streets, public areas, homelessness and housing programs. Revenue would stay in Ontario. The ballot measure requires audits and spending disclosure. The tax would continue until repealed by voters. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional 0.5% local sales and use tax.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not add this proposed 0.5% tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Extend San Bernardino County’s existing 0.5% transportation sales tax beginning April 1, 2040, after the current authorization ends March 31, 2040. This would not immediately increase the rate. The question estimates $250 million annually for the adopted road, highway, transit and transportation-technology plan. Revenue would stay under local control and be limited to transportation purposes, with audits, spending disclosure and independent taxpayer oversight. The extension has no fixed end; repeal requires a countywide voter decision and satisfaction of outstanding bond and contractual obligations. Approval requires a two-thirds vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Extend the existing 0.5% transportation tax from April 2040 under the new spending plan and oversight rules.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not approve this extension; the current authorization would still run through March 31, 2040.

parts.label: How the money would be divided
parts.what: After state collection fees, 3% is designated for interregional mobility, and 1% of net revenue for the administration fund. Remaining revenue is returned to the county’s subareas. In the Valley, 25% goes to local mobility, 50% regional mobility and 25% operations. In the Mountain and Desert subareas, the shares are 70%, 20% and 10%; additional transit operations may be funded from local mobility for unmet needs. Valley local shares use population; Mountain and Desert local shares use half population and half tax generation. Each jurisdiction reserves 5% of its local allocation for active transportation. After at least ten years, a jurisdiction may release that reserve if its governing body finds it unnecessary and the authority board approves.

parts.label: Spending and borrowing limits
parts.what: Tax-administration salaries and benefits cannot exceed the administration fund, which receives 1% of annual net tax revenue. Existing transportation funding must be maintained against the fiscal 2038–39 baseline, and this tax cannot replace development’s required fair share. The authority may borrow against future tax revenue, including before the extension begins, subject to the ordinance and its debt policy; outstanding principal cannot exceed estimated tax proceeds. Authority audits are biennial and local recipients’ audits annual.

parts.label: Changing the plan
parts.what: Plan changes cannot take effect before 2050. Reviews are required at least every ten years afterward, with public and local-jurisdiction input; amendments take effect 45 days after written notice to local jurisdictions and the county board. Changing subarea boundaries requires unanimous agreement of affected local jurisdictions. The measure also adjusts the constitutional spending limit by projected tax revenue.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Add a 1% Chino Hills sales and use tax, increasing the current combined rate from 7.75% to 8.75%. The city estimates $11.5 million annually for its general fund, available for any lawful city purpose, including public safety, wildfire preparation, open space, parks and streets. Groceries, prescription medicines, tuition, rent, utilities and generally labor and services would remain exempt. Collection would begin in the first calendar quarter more than 110 days after adoption, subject to state administration arrangements. The tax would continue until voters repeal it; the council could suspend all or part. Independent annual audits and public spending reports are required. Rate increases and expansion to new taxable transactions require voter approval. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional 1% local sales and use tax under these rules.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not add this proposed 1% tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Increase Needles’ tax on hotel, motel, recreational-vehicle and short-term lodging stays of 30 days or less from 10% to 12% on January 1, 2027, 13% on January 1, 2029 and 14% on January 1, 2030. Guests pay the tax and lodging operators collect it. The city estimates additional annual revenue of $200,000 at 12%, $300,000 at 13% and $400,000 at 14%, for its general fund and any lawful city purpose. The measure also updates monthly remittance and delinquency rules and requires annual public disclosure. It has no fixed expiration and would continue until ended by voters. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the phased lodging-tax increase and related collection rules.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep the current 10% lodging-tax rate rather than adopting this increase.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Authorize up to $11.2 million in Needles bonds for roads, streets and potholes, community safety, parks and recreation, and downtown Main Street improvements. Property taxes would repay principal and interest. The city estimates $739,971 annually, an average and highest rate of $60 per $100,000 of assessed value, and $25.16 million total repayment. These projections may vary and are not binding caps. Interest must stay within legal limits. Money must stay in Needles and cannot pay employee salaries or routine operating expenses. Annual financial and performance audits, independent citizen oversight, separate accounts and public reports are required. Approval requires a two-thirds vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Authorize the city to borrow up to $11.2 million for these improvements and levy property taxes to repay the bonds.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not authorize these bonds through this measure.

parts.label: Conflicting projected tax dates
parts.what: The official tax statement projects final tax collection in fiscal 2058–59, but also projects its highest rate through 2060–61. These inconsistent dates are estimates; taxes would be collected as needed while the bonds remain outstanding.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Revise Upland’s business-license tax starting January 1, 2027, with lower transition rates in 2027 and full rates in 2028. The first $100,000 of annual gross receipts would be subject only to a $75 minimum; receipts above that threshold would use rates based on business type. Self-storage facilities would also pay a per-unit amount. The schedule has an initial $28,000 annual maximum, with inflation adjustments described below. The city estimates $3.3 million total annual revenue, about $2.1 million more than the current tax, for general city services. Independent audits and public spending disclosure are required. This taxes businesses, including businesses operated by residents, rather than residency alone. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the revised business-license tax, transition rates, limits and exemptions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this proposed tax revision and keep the current business-license tax structure.

parts.label: Rates and inflation adjustments
parts.what: In 2027, rates on receipts above $100,000 would be 0.060% for retail and general commercial businesses, 0.100% for contractors, 0.125% for rentals and 0.090% for general or professional services. From 2028, the rates would be 0.065%, 0.150%, 0.200% and 0.125%, respectively. Self-storage facilities would also pay $50 per unit. The $75 minimum, $28,000 maximum and $50 per-unit amount would each rise with the applicable Consumer Price Index every January 1. The ordinance retains a separate tonnage-based tax for rock, sand and gravel extraction.

parts.label: Exemptions and veterans
parts.what: Businesses exempt under federal or state law remain exempt. An approved special-event vendor without a fixed city business or other city business activity may be exempt. Qualifying honorably discharged veterans unable to earn a livelihood through manual labor may obtain a free license with the required California voter eligibility and recent medical proof. Other honorably discharged veterans receive an application-fee waiver and a $100,000 gross-receipts credit, or the specified $108 business-tax credit, with proof of discharge. State-required fees cannot be waived.

parts.label: Future changes
parts.what: The council may amend or repeal the ordinance or reduce and later restore taxes within voter-approved limits. Increasing approved maximum rates or changing the tax method to increase the tax requires voter approval. The ballot question describes the tax as continuing until ended by voters; it has no fixed expiration.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Add a 1% Grand Terrace sales and use tax. The city estimates $1.2 million annually for its general fund, available for any lawful general city purpose, including police and emergency response. Groceries and prescription medicines remain exempt. Collection would begin in the first calendar quarter more than 110 days after adoption, subject to state administration arrangements. An advisory committee would review tax revenue, spending and annual audit reports and submit at least one written report a year to the council. Independent annual audits and public disclosure are required. The tax would continue until voters repeal it. The council could make administrative amendments, but a tax increase requires voter approval. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional 1% local tax and its oversight requirements.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not add this proposed 1% tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Change Colton’s city treasurer from an elected to an appointed office beginning November 7, 2028, or earlier if the current office becomes vacant. The current elected term would otherwise continue until that date. The council would appoint the treasurer, who would serve at its pleasure and would not have to be a city resident or registered voter. The council could delegate appointment authority to the city manager by ordinance. Later amendment or repeal of this measure would require voter approval. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve an appointed city treasurer under this transition and appointment process.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep the city treasurer as an elected office.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Add a 1% Adelanto sales and use tax beginning April 1, 2027. The city estimates $3 million annually for its general fund, available for any lawful municipal purpose, including streets, emergency services, public safety, parks, homelessness response and infrastructure. The tax applies to taxable purchases by residents and visitors; transactions exempt under existing law remain exempt. A transaction would pay the sales or use tax once, not both. Annual independent accountant audits must be reported publicly and posted on the city website. The tax has no fixed expiration and would continue until lawfully ended. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional 1% local sales and use tax and its audit requirements.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not add this proposed 1% tax.
